chapter: Callers: Papa John Joseph to Congo Square
title: Caller about her uncle Papa John Joseph
summary: After a calendar giveaway announcement, a niece recalls Papa John Joseph's Japan trip, his death while playing, and Allen tells where to find his records.

bands.name: Johnny Wiggs and His New Orleans Kings

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: This is WTIX 690, New Orleans, Louisiana. Here's Joe Collada.

Thank you very much, sir. Today's subject, jazz, Dixieland, whatever you want to call it, by one of the greats, Mr. Johnny Wiggins, Wiggs, I beg your pardon, sir, and by one of the true authorities in the country from Tulane University, Mr. Dick Allen. High Karate After Shave and Cologne presents Electric Train! Back in tune with more of Let's Talk It Over, we're going to get back in just a moment to Snoozer Quinn on My Melancholy Baby, and we'll have some comments on that by Mr. Johnny Wiggs of Johnny Wiggs and his New Orleans Kings and Mr. Dick Allen of Tulane. First, I want to tell you about something we're going to do. We do this sort of thing so seldom on Let's Talk It Over that we would like to make a big production out of it, but we don't make big productions out of anything here. Actually, Congressman F. Edward Hebert, who's been with us many, many times on Let's Talk It Over, last year gave us a calendar to give out from the House of Representatives. It's the official House of Representatives calendar, and so it was such a success. So many people wanted it that I understand not only, well, of course, we exhausted our supply in a very short time, but he exhausted his supply over at his office in a very short time. So what we're going to do this year is give 69 of the Congressman Hebert House of Representatives calendars to the first 69 people who write us either a letter or a postcard and give us their one wish, and there are many I'm sure we all have, for a happy new year. Whatever you would like to see come to pass in this new year, we'd like to know what you're thinking about. So your wish for a happy new year, 1970, a new decade, really. And we'll send the first 69 cards or letters which we receive here at WTIX, a Congressman F. Edward Hebert, House of Representatives calendar for the new year, truly a beautiful calendar. And I will add that the address, of course, is Let's Talk It Over, WTIX, New Orleans, Louisiana. Now that can be from the city or from out of town or wherever you're listening. For your House of Representatives calendar, given to us by Congressman F. Edward Hebert from the 1st District, send a postcard or a letter with your wish for a new year to WTIX, Let's Talk It Over, New Orleans, Louisiana. This is WTIX. Old Collada. Reminding you to stay tuned because at 11 o'clock, Archie Creech and Chip Kahn discuss the wonderful world of W.C. Fields. This hour, Mr. Johnny Wiggs of Johnny Wiggs and his New Orleans Kings and Mr. Dick Allen of Tulane University are discussing good, great music. Give us a call. Let's talk it over just as this lady's doing. Good morning. You're on the air. Good morning. Yes, ma'am. My name is Allen Nelson, and I want to talk to you concerning my uncle, Papa John Joseph. I didn't hear anything about him. He was one of these old musicians, one of the ones that were taken to Japan, I think in 87. Do you recall that? Mr. Dick Allen has it right here, and he's ready to give it to you. Really? Mm-hmm. Well, if she's interested in people knowing more about him, I can recommend, of course, his recordings, both of music and a taped interview. We have a taped interview with Papa John Joseph up at Tulane University there where he tells about his life because he's one of the musicians that played with all kind of jazz musicians. He even played rock and roll. I guess when he was up in his 80s, he played anything. He was a very, he was an excellent bass player. I hardly know where to start with a man like that. Played many, many instruments. And I wish I had known she was going to call out and brought some of his recordings down, say with George Lewis. Okay. Well, you know, he was one of the old Creoles from St. James Parish, and he played when he was a boy. They were four brothers, and they were all four musicians. There's one living now, Henry Joseph, and he lived in Donisonville. All other three is dead. That was Papa John Joseph, Nelson Joseph, and Willie Joseph. And when Papa John Joseph was about 87, I think it is, he went to Japan with all these old musicians, jazz musicians. He came back, and they gave a big birthday party for him in the French quarters. And they had a parade. Do you recall that? Oh, yes. I was there. Uh-huh. Well, I was one of the nieces that was walking with him. And they asked him at the time, how long would he like to play music? And he said he would like to play music until death. And if you remember, sometime in 92, I think it was, he played music down in French quarters every night. And that night he played When the Saints, When the Saints Go Marching In. And they asked him to play another version of it. And he started to play the other version of it, and as soon as that version was finished, he dropped. And that was the end of Papa John Joseph. I was in Little Rock with a bunch of the jazz musicians at that time, so I wasn't there that night, but I remember quite well when that happened. Uh-huh. Well, he really was one of the good old jazz players. He played every instrument there were, but he really stuck to the bass. You know, his brother Willie did record, too, with Louis Dumaine's Jazz Ola 8, I believe was the name of the band. Oh. A very good band there. And those recordings have been reissued. They're available on LP today, some of them. Uh-huh. Is there any way of my getting any of those records? I'll be glad to play them for you and give you the addresses of the different companies and places where you can write off. While I'm on the subject of where you can get records, if that young lady wants to write to George H. Buck for a copy of If Ever I Cease to Love, she can write to him at P.O. Box 748, Columbia, South Carolina. That's a Johnny Wiggs recording that somebody called in. Or else there's a place on Royal Street, isn't it, Johnny, that has a lot of records? They probably could get Papa John's records.
Yeah, I couldn't think of his last name, but I have thought of it. Tell him, Dick. Papa John Joseph.

It's Joe. Oh, this is Joe Sean. This is a record shop on. Oh, yes, uh-huh. Yeah, well, they could find his records. The shoppers were all there. They could find many, many jazz records there. Uh-huh. That's one of the places in town. Now, do you recall the time when Papa John Joseph played for the, uh, when John's son, uh, prisonership? And he played there, and he gave, uh, President Johnson one of, uh, gave President Johnson's daughter one of his records. Uh, well, I wasn't invited to that. I miss a lot of things. I see. He played it. He gave him one of his albums.
I love the way you put that thing.
